claims.text: Enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings results from synergistic intrinsic lattice distortion and interfacial barriers.
Intrinsic lattice distortion and multilayer interfaces jointly impede dislocation climb and glide.
Periodic interfaces locally alter stress fields.
Periodic interfaces slow atomic diffusion and thereby increase the activation energy for creep.
The as-fabricated multilayer coating has inherent lattice distortions.
The as-fabricated coating has a random or weakly ordered solid-solution phase.
Creep behavior can be tested by comparing a multilayer coating with a monolithic HEA coating of the same overall composition under identical conditions.
Lattice diffusion is active at elevated temperatures below the melting temperature.
Layer interfaces and lattice distortions produce local misfit strains and stress partitioning.
Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion can govern creep in an HEA.
The layered structure acts as a barrier to both dislocation glide and climb.
High configurational complexity increases lattice distortion and raises the energy barrier for dislocation motion under long-term loading.
Impeded dislocation motion reduces creep-strain accumulation.
Under identical high-temperature creep conditions, the multilayer coating will have a lower creep-strain rate and less total time-dependent deformation than the monolithic control.
Dislocation pile-ups or disruptions will be observed at layer interfaces.
The proposed mechanism applies when diffusion is non-negligible and layer thickness and interface coherency are optimized.
Temperatures approaching melting or very thick layers may diminish or alter the proposed interfacial mechanism.
Phase evolution or dynamic recrystallization during prolonged loading could affect creep behavior.
A lack of statistically significant creep-rate reduction or a lack of interfacial dislocation barriers relative to the monolithic control would falsify the hypothesis.
